methodology.identification: This study uses a comparative research approach to examine terrestrial environments that may serve as analogues for geological and environmental conditions on Mars and the Moon. It is based on the principle that certain geological processes and surface features observed on other planetary bodies can also be studied on Earth. The aim is to identify relevant similarities and understand how terrestrial observations can contribute to planetary research.
methodology.selection: Potential analogue locations were identified through existing scientific literature, geological studies, and planetary research databases. The search focuses on Earth environments that exhibit features comparable to those observed on Mars or the Moon, such as volcanic regions, impact craters, deserts, glacial environments, and other distinctive geological formations. Both previously studied analogue sites and locations with potential for further investigation are considered. Only locations with peer-reviewed scientific support for Moon or Mars relevance were included.
methodology.evidence:
Each location is examined using relevant geological and environmental characteristics. The study considers eight main parameters:

Geology: Rock types, mineral composition and geological formations.

Terrain: Landforms, surface structures and topography.

Temperature: Surface and environmental temperature conditions.

Water and ice: Presence, distribution and behaviour of water or ice.

Dust: Dust composition, movement and distribution.

Biology: Microbial life and the survival of organisms in extreme environments.

Subsurface: Underground geological structures and materials.

Human and robotic factors: Environmental and terrain conditions relevant to exploration activities.

The importance of each parameter varies depending on the planetary environment and the purpose of the comparison.
methodology.similarities: Available scientific observations and published research are used to compare the characteristics of terrestrial locations with those of their planetary counterparts. The assessment considers both similarities and differences, with particular attention to the geological processes and environmental conditions responsible for the observed features. Greater importance is given to comparisons supported by reliable scientific evidence. The findings are documented descriptively rather than expressed through an unvalidated numerical similarity score.
methodology.limitations: No terrestrial location can perfectly reproduce the conditions found on another planetary body. Differences in gravity, atmospheric pressure, radiation, temperature and geological history can influence the accuracy of comparisons. Furthermore, similar surface features may have formed through different processes. The assessment is also limited by the availability and quality of existing scientific information. Therefore, terrestrial analogues are treated as useful research references rather than exact representations of extraterrestrial environments. This dataset does not claim independent verification of every measurement; values are drawn from cited literature and may represent specific sampling sites rather than entire regions.

locations.name: Space Analog for the Moon and Mars (SAM), Biosphere 2
locations.description: A sealed, pressurised habitat vessel on the University of Arizona's Biosphere 2 campus, at the foot of the Santa Catalina Mountains. It has an airlock, engineering bay, crew quarters, a greenhouse and its own pressure-regulation system. The outdoor and indoor Mars yards were still being developed when the source table was written.
locations.setting: Biosphere 2 campus, base of the Santa Catalina Mountains.

targets.context: Mars yards for pressure-suit, rover and drone tests
Included because the facility is named for both targets; the source table lists only Mars-specific terrain entries.

geology.text: The Mars basalt dust was made from crushed volcanic rock from northern Arizona with very little original organic material, originally for the Biosphere 2 Landscape Evolution Observatory (LEO) experiment. The basalt bed is described as geologically accurate. Sedimentary and metamorphic terrain was added for variety.

terrain.text: A 12,000 sq ft (1,115 m2) outdoor Mars yard that is re-sculpted for each mission, and a 3,200 sq ft (300 m2) indoor yard with fine-grained basalt beds. A synthetic lava tube was being built in autumn 2023.

subsurface.text: Synthetic lava tube under construction (autumn 2023, per the source).

exploration.text: Pressurised suits are used for every EVA. The indoor yard has a gravity off-set rig for reduced gravity. The habitat is sealed, with delayed communications and an on-site mission control.

mars.similarities: Basalt terrain beds built to be geologically accurate, plus a crushed-basalt dust, set up for suited EVA, rover and drone work.

relevance.robotic: Rover and drone tests in the Mars yards.
relevance.human: Long confinement in a sealed habitat with delayed communications; suited EVA in the yards.

locations.name: Haughton impact structure, Devon Island
locations.elevation: Crater basin about 140 m; surrounding annular ridge about 270 m; regional plateau 340-400 m
locations.description: A roughly 23 km (apparent diameter) impact structure in the Canadian Arctic, formed about 39 million years ago. A hydrothermal system followed the impact, and later lake sediments filled part of the crater. NASA's Haughton-Mars Project has worked here since 1997, and the Mars Society's FMARS station sits on Haynes Ridge overlooking it.
locations.setting: Polar desert near the north coast of Devon Island, about 165 km northeast of Resolute. The table notes a boat is needed to reach the island and the crater.

targets.environment: Early Mars (impact craters, crater lakes, hydrothermal alteration)
targets.context: Grouped under Early Mars in Preston & Dartnell (2014).
The table compares the crater with Shackleton Crater, a 19 km wide impact crater at the lunar south pole.

geology.text: Shales, quartz-bearing rocks and allochthonous breccia. The crater-fill impact melt breccias have a calcite-anhydrite-silicate glass groundmass. The impact heated the crater fill and drove a hydrothermal system, described as a transient warm, wet microbial oasis.

terrain.text: Loose rock, craters, rock glaciers, gullies, sapping valleys, valley networks and canyons.

temperature.text: Cold polar desert; the table notes cold temperatures but gives no figures.

water.text: Ground ice and permafrost. Breccia at the crater centre is permeated with permafrost, which is the feature compared with ice-bearing craters on Mars.

biology.text: Hydrothermal gypsum hosts endolithic cyanobacterial communities.

exploration.text: EVA in Earth gravity in a remote, unequipped, isolated setting. NASA has run missions here since 1997.

mars.similarities: Ground ice, rock glaciers, gullies, valley networks, an ancient crater lake and hot-spring deposits are all listed as Mars-relevant features. Preston & Dartnell group it with Early Mars analogues for impact craters, crater-lake deposits and hydrothermal alteration.

moon.similarities: Compared with Shackleton Crater, the 19 km impact crater at the Moon's south pole.

relevance.application: Test site for planetary exploration strategies in a cold, dry, rocky environment.
relevance.human: Haughton-Mars Project missions since 1997 test technology and operations in a remote, extreme environment.

locations.evidenceNotes: Elevations are from Robertson & Mason (1975): 140 m for the inner basin, 270 m for the ridge, 340-400 m regionally. The structure's age is quoted differently across sources (about 39 Ma in Osinski et al. 2005, younger in older work); the 39 Ma value is used here. Diameter varies too: roughly 16 km for the final crater, about 23 km apparent.

locations.name: Svalbard (AMASE study area)
locations.description: An Arctic volcanic region that NASA has used since 2003 for the Arctic Mars Analog Svalbard Expedition (AMASE). The coordinate in the source table is a general point for the archipelago, not a single field site. Preston & Dartnell single out the Bockfjord Volcanic Complex, with three eruptive centres spread over more than 20 km.
locations.setting: High-latitude glacial and volcanic landscape with very low temperatures.

targets.environment: Middle Mars (polar habitats, carbonates, volcanoes, gullies)
targets.context: Grouped under Middle Mars in Preston & Dartnell (2014).
The table lists red sandstone and volcanic rocks (basalt) under the Moon column.

terrain.text: Rocky ground, rough field, rock glaciers, a volcanic centre, hot springs, perennial rivers, and folds. Glacial setting with gullies.

temperature.text: Very low temperatures; no figures given in the table.

water.text: Glacial environment; microbial activity has been found within blue ice at Bockfjord.

biology.text: Methanogens and psychrophiles at Bockfjord; extremophiles adapted to extreme cold.

exploration.text: EVA in Earth gravity in an isolated setting. The table describes a confinement exercise with no communication between two teams.

mars.similarities: Preston & Dartnell list carbonates, polar habitats, fluvial features, gullies, volcanoes, hot springs and biosignatures as the Mars-relevant features at Bockfjord.

moon.similarities: Basalt is the listed lunar match.

locations.description: A natural acid rock drainage system whose river water is about pH 3.2 and carries iron sulphates and oxides. Iron-oxidising, acid-tolerant bacteria dominate the microbial community. The site is easy to reach, next to a main road and a town.

targets.environment: Early Mars (iron oxides and sulphates, past river channels)
targets.context: Grouped under Early Mars in Preston & Dartnell (2014).

biology.text: Aerobic extremophile bacteria and chemolithotrophic microorganisms; the community is dominated by iron-oxidising, acid-tolerant bacteria.

locations.name: Atacama Desert (hyperarid core)
locations.elevation: About 970 m at the Yungay halite sampling sites; the elevation changes a lot across the desert
locations.description: The hyperarid core of the Atacama is among the driest places on Earth, with highly saline soils rich in perchlorates and the strongest UV irradiation on Earth. Some sites, such as Maria Elena South, are described as being as dry as Mars. It is used to test rovers and life-detection instruments.
locations.setting: Desert between the Pacific coast range and the Andes. The Yungay area sits in the hyperarid core.

targets.environment: Present Mars (Mars-like soils, perchlorates, aridity, UV)
targets.context: Grouped under Present Mars in Preston & Dartnell (2014).

geology.text: Perchlorate-rich volcanic soils. Soils in the core are saline and oxidising and very low in organic material. The table also notes the otherworldly look of the soil.

terrain.text: Playas, volcanic terrain and impact deposits are listed as relevant landforms.

temperature.text: The table lists extreme temperatures but gives no figures. UV radiation is the highest on Earth (table).

water.text: Less than 2 mm of precipitation a year in the driest areas (Preston & Dartnell).

biology.text: Low bacterial levels in the soils. Endolithic photosynthetic microbes live in halite crusts and pore spaces. A subsurface microbial oasis was found about two metres below the surface with a life-detector chip instrument (Parro et al. 2011).

exploration.text: Rovers and life-detection drills have been tested here, including a NASA drill test in 2016.

mars.similarities: Perchlorate-bearing, saline, oxidising soils with very little organic matter; extreme dryness and UV; halite endoliths as a habitability case.

relevance.application: Ground-truthing for life-detection instruments and soil chemistry before Mars missions.
relevance.robotic: Used for testing rovers, drills and life-detection equipment.

locations.name: Lonar Crater (Lonar Lake impact structure)
locations.description: A roughly 1.8 km crater excavated in the basalt of the Deccan Traps and one of only two known terrestrial craters formed in basalt. Drill cores from the crater floor contain impact breccias altered by a post-impact hydrothermal system.
locations.setting: Deccan Traps basalt plateau; the crater holds a lake. Marker placed at the approximate centre of the structure.

targets.environment: Impact craters in basaltic crust; impact-induced hydrothermal alteration
targets.context: Proposed by Hagerty & Newsom (2003) as an analogue for similarly sized craters on Mars, and as a lower size limit for impact-driven hydrothermal clay formation.

targets.environment: Small impact crater in a basaltic target (interpretive)
targets.context: Basalt is the lunar mare target rock; no lunar-specific study of Lonar was read, so this link rests on target lithology only.

geology.text: Target rock is Deccan Traps basalt (about 65 Ma according to Hagerty & Newsom). Core samples from the crater floor are altered basaltic impact breccias in which the main secondary mineral is Fe-rich saponite, with minor celadonite and carbonate. Thermodynamic modelling and comparison with volcanic analogues suggest the clays formed at roughly 130-200 C.

terrain.text: Bowl-shaped simple crater about 1.8 km across, about 50,000 years old in the age used by Hagerty & Newsom.

water.text: The crater holds a lake. No hydrochemistry was taken from the sources read.

subsurface.text: Hydrothermal alteration is documented in drill core from beneath the crater floor, not at the surface.

mars.earthObservations: Hagerty & Newsom (2003) describe saponite-dominated alteration of basaltic breccia in cores from the crater floor, with minor celadonite and carbonate, formed at about 130-200 C by a post-impact hydrothermal system.
mars.planetaryObservations: The same paper compares Lonar's basalt composition with martian basaltic meteorites and models that alteration in 2-11 km craters could sequester about 0.7 m of water as a global layer over Mars' history. That figure is a model estimate by the authors, not a measurement.
mars.similarities: Basaltic target rock, a crater small enough to be representative of the many small martian craters, and an Fe-rich clay assemblage of the kind that could add iron-bearing phases to martian soil.
mars.differences: The Lonar hydrothermal system depended on liquid water near the surface, which the authors treat as a condition for Mars rather than a given. Lonar is geologically very young compared with most martian craters, and the Deccan Traps are not a direct match for any specific martian terrain.

moon.similarities: Basaltic target; lunar mare craters also form in basalt.
moon.differences: Lonar has surface water, an atmosphere and weathering, none of which exist on the Moon, and hydrothermal clay formation has no established lunar counterpart.

relevance.application: Ground truth for recognising impact-hydrothermal clay alteration in basaltic craters.

Age is quoted from Hagerty & Newsom; the age of Lonar has been debated and is not resolved here. The Moon target is interpretive. Elevation not verified.
